question: Roughly what percentage of whole blood is made up of plasma?
explanation: Spot on! Plasma is the straw-colored liquid part of your blood, making up just over half (about 55%) of your total blood volume. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h1)

question: When blood spins in a centrifuge, a tiny middle layer forms between the plasma and red blood cells. What is this 'buffy coat' made of?
explanation: You got it! That thin buffy coat mainly contains your infection-fighting white blood cells and tiny platelets that help blood to clot. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which of these is a key way your blood helps regulate your body?

options.B: Generating electrical impulses for the heart
options.D: Producing red bone marrow stem cells

explanation: Well done! Blood acts like a personal heating system, picking up heat from active muscles and sharing it around the body to keep you at a steady, safe temperature. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h2)

question: How does your blood protect your body against germs and infections?

options.A: By increasing the total volume of red blood cells
options.B: By filtering toxins directly through the skin
options.C: By lowering blood pressure during an illness
options.D: By circulating white blood cells and antibodies

explanation: Exactly! Your bloodstream acts like a highway, rushing white blood cells and antibodies straight to wherever germs are trying to attack. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which major plasma protein keeps fluid inside your blood vessels by pulling in water?
explanation: Great job! Albumin is the most abundant protein in plasma. It acts like a sponge, holding water inside the blood vessels so it doesn't leak out into tissues. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the main difference between blood plasma and serum?

options.A: Plasma is found outside blood vessels while serum is found inside
options.B: Plasma contains red blood cells while serum contains only white blood cells
options.C: Serum lacks clotting proteins like fibrinogen because it has already clotted
options.D: Serum has a much higher water content than plasma

explanation: Spot on! Think of serum as plasma that has finished doing its clotting job; the clotting proteins (like fibrinogen) get used up during the clot, leaving serum behind. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h3)

question: What special shape helps red blood cells squeeze through tiny blood vessels and carry plenty of oxygen?
explanation: You nailed it! Their unique biconcave shape (flattened donuts without holes) gives them a massive surface area and makes them super flexible to squeeze through tight spots. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h4)

question: What tells your kidneys to release erythropoietin (EPO) to make more red blood cells?

options.A: High blood pressure in the arteries
options.C: Low oxygen levels in the blood

explanation: Correct! When your kidneys sense your body isn't getting quite enough oxygen, they send out EPO like an alarm bell to tell your bone marrow to pump out more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which white blood cell is the most common and acts as the quick-response team against bacteria?
explanation: Well done! Neutrophils make up the biggest percentage of your white blood cells and are usually the very first heroes to arrive at a bacterial infection site. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is it called when white blood cells squeeze right through tiny blood vessel walls to reach an infection?
explanation: Spot on! Diapedesis is just the medical term for white blood cells slipping out of the bloodstream into the tissues to fight off trouble. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h5)

question: Platelets break off from which giant cells found in the bone marrow?
explanation: You got it! Megakaryocytes are massive cells in your bone marrow that literally pinch off bits of themselves to create platelets. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the final goal of the blood clotting (coagulation) cascade?

options.A: Breakdown of mature red blood cells by spleen macrophages
options.B: Conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads
options.C: Release of erythropoietin from the renal cortex
options.D: Rapid constriction of smooth muscle in the heart ventricles

explanation: Brilliant! The whole clotting chain reaction ends by turning liquid fibrinogen into a tough, solid net of fibrin fibers that seals up the cut. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal red blood cell donor because it has no A or B antigens?
explanation: Correct! Because Type O red blood cells don't carry A or B antigens, a recipient's immune system won't easily attack them during emergencies. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h7)

question: What happens when someone gets a transfusion of the wrong, incompatible blood type?

options.A: The recipient's bone marrow stops producing new hemoglobin
options.B: Plasma proteins dissolve all white blood cells in the sample
options.C: Donor red blood cells undergo agglutination and hemolysis
options.D: Platelets instantly multiply to repair the blood vessels

explanation: You nailed it! The recipient's antibodies attack the foreign blood cells, causing them to clump together (agglutinate) and break apart (hemolysis). [learn more](GNS311_U2_T1#GNS311_U2_T1_h7)
